verses.text: The word which came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, when king Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur the son of Malchijah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest, saying,
“Please inquire of Yahweh for us; for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon makes war against us. Perhaps Yahweh will deal with us according to all his wondrous works, that he may withdraw from us.”
Then Jeremiah said to them, “Tell Zedekiah:

‘Yahweh, the God of Israel says, “Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands, with which you fight against the king of Babylon, and against the Chaldeans who besiege you, without the walls; and I will gather them into the middle of this city.
I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, even in anger, and in wrath, and in great indignation.
I will strike the inhabitants of this city, both man and animal. They will die of a great pestilence.

Afterward,” says Yahweh, “I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah, and his servants, and the people, even those who are left in this city from the pestilence, from the sword, and from the famine, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those who seek their life. He will strike them with the edge of the sword. He will not spare them, neither have pity, nor have mercy.”’
“To this people you shall say, ‘Yahweh says: “Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.

He who remains in this city will die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence; but he who goes out, and passes over to the Chaldeans who besiege you, he shall live, and he will escape with his life.
For I have set my face on this city for evil, and not for good,” says Yahweh. “It will be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.”’
“Concerning the house of the king of Judah, hear Yahweh’s word.

House of David, Yahweh says, ‘Execute justice in the morning, and deliver him who is robbed out of the hand of the oppressor, lest my wrath go out like fire, and burn so that no one can quench it, because of the evil of your doings.
Behold, I am against you, O inhabitant of the valley, and of the rock of the plain,’ says Yahweh. ‘You that say, “Who would come down against us?” or “Who would enter into our homes?”
I will punish you according to the fruit of your doings, says Yahweh; and I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it shall devour all that is around her.’”

footnotes.content: Zedekiah is desperate enough to send for Jeremiah, the man he'd imprisoned for his hard prophecies. There's a longing in that message—a king hoping a prophet might soften God's answer. But the Lord is closer than ever, even in judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Perhaps Yahweh will deal with us according to all his wondrous works." Even cornered, Zedekiah reaches for hope—he recalls God's mighty deeds. Yet this prayer skips repentance. We too sometimes ask for rescue while holding tight to our own way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah doesn't refuse. He's told to pass on what the Lord will say—a messenger who stays faithful even when the message breaks hearts. Faithfulness sometimes means speaking what will wound.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will turn back the weapons of war." The promise Zedekiah longed for is flipped: the very tools meant to protect will be gathered into the city itself. When we resist God's direction, our defenses become our trap. Babylon's siege was not the final blow—the Lord's own turning was.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I myself will fight against you." The outstretched hand and strong arm that once sheltered Israel now turn in judgment. When the Judge Himself becomes the adversary, all earthly armies pale. This is mercy too—a God who will not pretend indifference to rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pestilence strikes both man and animal—the scope of judgment is total. No refuge in armies, no negotiation. Yet even here, if we look beyond the judgment, God is still God. He does not lose control; He does not forget His own purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah and his people are delivered into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, without pity or mercy. Hard words—but they name a hard truth. The king had rejected warnings repeatedly. Sometimes the Lord withdraws His hand to let us reap what we've sown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The way of life and the way of death." This is Deuteronomy's echo—Moses also set these before Israel. The Lord always leaves a choice open, even in siege. Surrender to the enemy and live; stay in the city and die. The mercy is hidden, but it's there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He that goes out and passes over to the Chaldeans...shall live." An unbearable choice—abandon your city, your king, your own people to find life? Yet the Lord makes clear which door leads to life. Sometimes humility means walking through the door pride says is shameful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have set my face on this city for evil." God's face—His attention, His resolve—is fixed. The fire will burn. Yet even judgment is not the last word; it opens a door to repentance and renewal, if the people will walk through it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A shift now—from judgment on the people to a word for "the house of the king." Even in ruin, the Lord addresses the throne. Leadership carries a special summons: to execute justice and defend the robbed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "House of David, execute justice in the morning." Morning—the first light, the place where new choices begin. A king could still turn: deliver the robbed from oppression, or face the fire of God's wrath. Even Jerusalem's final hours held open an invitation to righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You who say, 'Who would come down against us?'" Pride speaks first. The valley, the rock—natural strength, city walls, the illusion of unassailable security. But the Lord's question is already answered: He Himself will come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it shall devour all that is around her." Readers today hear an echo: how often the Lord allows our own works to consume us, until in the ash we finally turn to Him. Not punishment alone, but a terrible mercy that breaks us open to His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
